tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop

- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

input.task:
Repo: Moneo (Next.js 16 App Router personal finance app). Read AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/measure-speed/SKILL.md first and follow them strictly (no code comments, surgical changes, money numbers must stay identical, commit each step).

Goal: make every page other than Home lighter and faster to open, both on first open after the app starts and on in-app navigation. Measured (production QA build, warm): server full render Settings ~216 ms, Plan ~224 ms, Transactions ~165 ms, Wealth ~139 ms, Accounts ~118 ms; client JS per page: Settings 536 KB, Plan 421 KB, Transactions 282 KB, Ask (/ai) 284 KB, others ~170 KB; long tasks Settings 5/369 ms, Plan 4/307 ms. Pages: /ai, /ai/artifacts, /ai/activity, /money/accounts, /money/transactions, /money/recurring, /money/wealth, /plan, /plan/spending, /settings.

Approach: for each heavy page find what ships to the client (big client components, libraries like echarts, dnd-kit, react-markdown, tanstack table, lucide icons, zod on the client) and what the server waits on (log the PostgREST query waterfall by temporarily timing supabaseFetch in lib/supabase-fetch.ts — never commit that). Lazy-load client parts that aren't needed for first paint, stream slow sections behind their own Suspense with stable-size fallbacks (CLS must not get worse), dedupe repeated reads, start independent reads together. Also check client-side navigation between pages (prefetch behaviour, loading.tsx, staleTimes in next.config.ts — note: staleTimes.dynamic was deliberately tuned before; a previous attempt made back navigation slower, so measure back navigation too). Respect `npm run check:bundle` budgets (lower them if you shrink pages a lot).

Measure with production builds on the moneo-qa backend: yours on `QA_PORT=3131 npm run qa:server -- --production`, a base build of branch t3/speed-build-and-startup in a separate worktree on port 3132 (never port 3000 or the owner's .env); `node scripts/perf-pages.mjs 5 before=http://localhost:3132 after=http://localhost:3131`. Machine is noisy: interleave and repeat.

Open a PR with `gh pr create --base t3/speed-build-and-startup` (NOT main) with a before/after Speed table per page (heading time desktop+mobile, JS KB, server render), screenshots of visibly changed pages (skill verify-ui / npm run qa:shots), and what didn't help. Run npm test, npm run lint, npm run typecheck, npm run build, npm run check:bundle before. Stop servers you started (by port + checkout path). Last line: PR <url>, head <sha>, checks <state>.

cat > "C:/Users/mgsuk/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/db59e4d2c3a36d77/396b32a3-bfbf-4e71-9897-515e591c4f32/scratchpad/pr318.md" <<'EOF'
Makes Moneo faster to build, check, start and open: the build, CI, the desktop app's start, every page request, Home and the first chat answer. Merged here: my commits plus sub-PRs #319, #320 and #321.

## Gains

| What | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `next build`, warm (local) | 50 s | 23 s |
| `next build` TypeScript phase, cold | 101 s | skipped (`npm run typecheck` does it) |
| `npm run typecheck` (local, median) | 129 s | 54 s |
| CI build job | 165 s | 41 s |
| CI browser job | 248 s | 112 s |
| CI test job | 105 s | 32 s |
| CI typecheck job | 88 s | 37 s |
| Page time to first byte (every page, warm) | ~95 ms | ~35 ms |
| Accounts, full server render | 207 ms | ~118 ms |
| Home, full server render (warm) | 208 ms | 150 ms |
| Home heading after a server start | 1,281 ms | 774 ms |
| Desktop app: Home usable on a normal start | 6.4 s | 3.8 s |
| Desktop app: Next server ready | 4.9 s | 1.8 s |
| Desktop app: first run | 17.0 / 38.6 s | 15.6 / 28.8 s |
| New chat, send to first text, cold (AI mocked) | 587 ms | 536 ms |

The CI "before" numbers come from a run whose dependency cache missed. That miss is one of the things fixed here (see the CI cache change below), so the comparison is fair. Desktop memory and process count are unchanged (~1.48 GB, 34 processes).

## What changed

**Build and checks**
- `next build` no longer runs its own type check, which only repeated `npm run typecheck`. `typecheck` now runs `next typegen` first, so route types are still checked.
- Type checking uses the native TypeScript 7 compiler for the app and desktop projects. The three checks run in parallel and keep incremental caches in CI (#319). Injected type, indexed-access, lint and feature-map errors still fail.
- Lint prechecks run without nested npm start-up. The feature map scans the source in one pass.
- The CI `node_modules` cache is keyed on the lockfile only, so editing an npm script no longer forces `npm ci` (50–80 s) in every job. A cache miss now installs from the npm download cache.

**Every request**
- The backend signs session tokens with HS256. Supabase's `getClaims()` therefore called GoTrue `/auth/v1/user` (~60 ms) in the proxy and again in `requireWorkspace` on every page, action and API call. The token's signature is now checked on the server with `JWT_SECRET`. A token that fails the check still goes to GoTrue, and `requireWorkspace` still confirms the user with GoTrue once a minute. The desktop app passes `JWT_SECRET` to its Next server.
- The Claude Code provider and agent SDK load only when a Claude model runs, so they're no longer compiled on every server start.

**Home and chat (#321)**
- The Home heading streams on its own. Independent widget reads start earlier, and loan, budget and agent-run data is shared within one render (71 → 68 queries).
- Money and date formatters are reused instead of rebuilt for every figure. Output is identical: rendered figures matched the previous build in all eight default widgets, on desktop and mobile.
- Chat starts its read-only setup alongside creating the conversation. Attachment parsers and optional modules load only when used, and title generation starts once the answer is under way.

**Desktop start (#320)**
- GoTrue, Storage and PostgREST start together once Postgres is up. The Next server and the bank certificate start as soon as the ports are chosen. Readiness checks every 50 ms instead of 250 ms.
- In the desktop app, background work (workflow recovery, scheduler, bank listener) waits for a `moneo:backend-ready` message. The message is sent again if the Next server restarts. The source install is unchanged.
- The owner is looked up in `auth.users` instead of being posted to GoTrue on every start.
- Each start-up step logs its duration to `backend.log` and `main.log`.
- The pre-upgrade backup still runs before any service starts; this was checked by forcing a service version change. `desktop:smoke` passes all 27 checks.

## Tried and dropped (no measurable gain)
- Node's compile cache.

content.content:
## 4. Evidence

- Use the path the owner uses: real pages, real buttons. Not a test-only endpoint or a direct database write for the step under test.
- Capture the action and the state it leaves, not only the last screen.
- Check the side effects next to what is visible: the row written, the history entry, what undo restores.
- **Look at every picture yourself.** Read each PNG. Check for overflow, clipped text, unreadable contrast in dark and a broken layout on mobile. A console error or a status of 400 or more is a failure: fix it and shoot again.
- When something looks wrong, suspect the capture before the app, and measure the live page before reporting a bug.

## 5. Hand over

The pictures go in the PR description itself, so the owner sees them on GitHub. A path to `.qa/` is not evidence: it is git-ignored and exists only on this machine. Never commit them to the PR's branch either.

1. Open the PR first to get its number.
2. Push the files to their own branch, `pr-assets/<pr>`, which holds nothing else. The repo is public, so QA data only:

   ```sh
   git worktree add --orphan -b pr-assets/<pr> .qa/pr-assets
   cp -r .qa/shots/before .qa/shots/after .qa/pr-assets/
   git -C .qa/pr-assets add -A
   git -C .qa/pr-assets commit -m "Screenshots for #<pr> (QA data)"
   git -C .qa/pr-assets push origin pr-assets/<pr>
   git worktree remove .qa/pr-assets
   ```

   To add more later, check the branch out again with `git worktree add .qa/pr-assets pr-assets/<pr>`.
3. Embed them with `gh pr edit <pr> --body-file <file>`, before and after side by side in a table, one row per page and view that visibly changed, with one line on what to look at:

   ```markdown
   | Before | After |
   | --- | --- |
   | ![Home, dark, before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/indkhan/Moneo/pr-assets/<pr>/before/home-dark.png) | ![Home, dark, after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/indkhan/Moneo/pr-assets/<pr>/after/home-dark.png) |
   ```

4. **A flow:** GitHub plays a GIF inline but not a video from a branch. If `ffmpeg` is installed, turn the recording into a GIF and embed it: `ffmpeg -i video.webm -vf "fps=10,scale=900:-1" flow.gif`. Otherwise embed a screenshot of each key state. Either way, push the recording too (`video.webm` from `test-results/`) and link it.
5. Open the PR on GitHub and check that every image shows.

Say which pages you covered, what changed in each and what you could not capture and why. If nothing visibly changed, say so and attach nothing.

## 6. Clean up
